name: Genre Awareness

objectives.text: Identify whether a Bible passage read aloud is a story or a song
Recognize that the Bible is one book made up of many kinds of writing, such as stories, songs, laws, and letters
Distinguish a law that tells God's people what to do from a letter written to a church
Identify picture words in a psalm and tell what each picture teaches about God
Explain that a parable is a story Jesus told to teach a truth about God's kingdom
Distinguish history writing that reports what happened from prophecy that delivers God's message through a prophet
Sort the books of the Bible into their main genres, including law, history, poetry and wisdom, prophecy, gospel, epistle, and apocalyptic
Explain that the Gospels are historical accounts of Jesus written so that readers may know and believe the truth about him
Compare how a reader should handle a psalm of praise with how a reader should handle a commandment
Identify the features of a parable, such as an everyday setting, a central point, and a surprising twist
Identify synonymous, contrasting, and building parallelism in lines of Hebrew poetry
Describe common forms of prophetic speech, such as the covenant lawsuit, the woe oracle, and the promise of restoration
Describe the standard parts of a New Testament letter, including greeting, thanksgiving, body, and closing
Explain why proverbs state general patterns of wise living rather than unconditional promises
Interpret figures of speech such as metaphor, hyperbole, and anthropomorphism in poetic and prophetic passages without reading them in a wooden literal way
Apply guidelines for reading apocalyptic literature, including interpreting symbols, numbers, and visions by the explanations the text itself provides
Analyze how the structure of a lament psalm moves from complaint to petition to trust and praise
Explain how the occasional nature of the epistles, written to answer specific questions and problems, shapes the way they are interpreted
Distinguish descriptive narrative from prescriptive teaching and explain why a narrative that reports an action does not necessarily commend it
Analyze the forms of Old Testament law and explain the Reformed tradition's distinction between moral, ceremonial, and judicial law
Evaluate interpretations that classify biblical narratives as myth by examining the genre markers of historical writing in the text
Evaluate how speeches within dialogue wisdom books such as Job and Ecclesiastes must be read in light of the book's overall design and conclusion
Analyze passages where genres are blended, such as a victory song set within a narrative, and explain how each genre contributes to the passage's meaning
Create a genre analysis of a chosen biblical book that identifies its genres, literary features, and the interpretive guidelines they require

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (story vs song, law vs letter, picture words, parables, history vs prophecy, sorting books by genre, psalm vs commandment, parallelism, apocalyptic, proverbs as patterns, epistles as occasional, descriptive vs prescriptive, historicity vs myth, book-level synthesis). Dropped the vague recall item and the genre-to-purpose item, which belongs to Authorial Intent. Moved the epistle item down and made it explanatory rather than a vague hermeneutic. Added Gospel genre, parable features, prophetic speech forms, epistle structure, figures of speech, lament structure, the forms of Old Testament law with the Reformed threefold distinction (WCF 19.3-5), dialogue wisdom books, and blended genres. Replaced whole-text citations with specific verse ranges throughout.
